beats.trigger: ## Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)
beats.got: Title only; the module is about agents making agents.

beats.trigger: The tool that builds tools compounds.
beats.got: Nothing new yet. It is a slogan, and I want to see whether it holds.

beats.trigger: Revisit the crux, what would have to be true, pre-mortem.
beats.got: Nothing new. Reminders of earlier modules, with no pointer to where they are.

beats.trigger: **Produce** a strategy kernel, suggested agent set, and two-week plan from your files
beats.got: The output is a kernel, an agent set and a plan, which I could take to the pricing group.

beats.trigger: The question to carry through: where is all this going?
beats.got: Setup for a shared folder with one folder per person. Fine, but it is logistics.

beats.trigger: **Agent generates agent.** You watch one agent build another on real input.
beats.got: Short and clear. I will see it in the exercise.

beats.trigger: Pick one extension you'd use from Tuesday onward:
beats.got: Three kinds of extension: new source, new output, new perspective. I would pick perspective, a skeptic for my pricing sources.

beats.trigger: On Mondays I need to Y; today I Z by hand.
beats.got: A four-line brief. This is the spec, and writing it forces me to say what I actually need.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "extend-your-system-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: Claude built the agent file from my brief. I paste a prompt and wait, so not much for me to do here.

beats.trigger: "You used training data on line 4. Replace it or remove it."
beats.got: Judging the output and pushing back is where the quality comes from, and it is a skill in its own right.

beats.trigger: Monday's new gap gets a new agent in 25 minutes, not a new sprint.
beats.got: A new gap gets a new agent in 25 minutes. I believe it for one agent, and I doubt it for fourteen people.

beats.trigger: Twenty agents publish into the shared deliberation folder.
beats.got: A big room exercise, nine stages, 70 minutes. Impressive on paper. I wonder whether my team could run it.

beats.trigger: Every claim in every later round cites the file it came from.
beats.got: Every claim cites its source file, and that is the right discipline. The redaction warning is sensible for a Nordic legal team.

beats.trigger: Do not read other participants' stances yet: different context, sources, and judgment make the first round useful.
beats.got: Stances are written independently first, so they do not all converge on one view.

beats.trigger: Find what your stance missed.
beats.got: The agent reads neighbours' stances and finds my blind spots. Useful if it surfaces a real contradiction.

beats.trigger: The file history shows who changed their mind and why.
beats.got: Proposals go into the shared folder. Another prompt paste.

beats.trigger: Do not average the room.
beats.got: The synthesizer is told to choose rather than average. I like that, since averaging is what committees do.

beats.trigger: From here on, every agent prompt begins by reading `midway-instructions.md` from the shared folder.
beats.got: The synthesizer steers all the agents through a file. It is clever, but I am not sure why I need it.

beats.trigger: The selection board is the candidate, not final.
beats.got: Everyone attacks the selection before it is final, which is a proper review round.

beats.trigger: The human picks.
beats.got: The agents produce the options and a person decides which assumptions to test. That is how I run my team too.

beats.trigger: Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:
beats.got: Three files at the end: kernel, agent set, plan.

beats.trigger: Likeliest unseen pre-mortem failure; one early warning sign.
beats.got: The kernel has diagnosis, policy, experiments with owner and success signal, and risks. I could show that to my CFO.

beats.trigger: "You are now agent builders."
beats.got: A scripted sponsor sentence that tells me what I am. It is a bit much, and I would not say it to my team.

beats.trigger: Pushback rounds were the work.
beats.got: It did not converge on the first try, and the pushback was the useful part. That makes it more believable.

beats.trigger: Four observations and two questions follow.
beats.got: A reflective lecture follows the exercise.

beats.trigger: What changed is who assembles them, and specifying well is the harder half.
beats.got: The hard part is specifying well. The assembly is done for me, and writing a clever prompt is not the skill.

beats.trigger: Access was instant and complete. What the room took up from each other is the smaller number.
beats.got: Having access to everything is not the same as using it. Count the folders cited, because that is my rollout number for the board.

beats.trigger: Without that rule, agents reading agents invent each other's sources
beats.got: Same point as phase 1: agents must cite. Said a second time.

beats.trigger: The plan names the wall your company hits first: data access, runtime platform, or discoverability.
beats.got: There are three walls: data access, runtime platform, discoverability. Mine is probably discoverability, since nobody knows where the context files are.

beats.trigger: The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.
beats.got: The parts stay stable while the model changes. A reasonable reassurance.

beats.trigger: Nobody in this room knows yet, and the people running this training do not know either.
beats.got: The trainers admit they do not know what will be obsolete. That is the understatement I trust more than a promise.

beats.trigger: What your company knows about its own work gets better only when somebody writes it down and somebody else picks it up.
beats.got: The model improves for free, but my company's knowledge only improves if someone writes it down and someone else picks it up. That is the shared-place problem I have.

beats.trigger: If nobody can answer, you have a belief with a schedule attached.
beats.got: Ask what would make us drop the plan. If nobody can answer, it is a belief and not a plan.

beats.trigger: The kernel came out of the same move as your first briefing: agents read, agents argued, something chose, and nothing in the room checked it.
beats.got: Nothing checked the kernel, so I should hold doubt about it. That is honest.

beats.trigger: Precision compounds. So does blur.
beats.got: The agent reviews the session and rewrites the key file in place. Edit one section, do not rewrite the whole file.

beats.trigger: The agent audits itself, so the summary is not neutral.
beats.got: An agent's self-audit is not neutral, so ask it for a critique it ignored.

beats.trigger: Agents must cite each other's files, or they invent what they never read.
beats.got: Nothing new. Recap.

beats.trigger: You leave with a flywheel, not a graduation.
beats.got: Nothing new. The flywheel line is repeated and the ending is a bit grand.

take_homes: Specifying clearly is the hard part. The agent builds, I judge and push back.
Access is not uptake. I count how many shared folders actually get cited and use that as my rollout number.
Every agent claim must cite its source file, and I ask 'what would make us drop this?' of any plan.

monday.move: Write a four-line extension brief for a skeptic agent that reads my pricing-pilot sources and flags where they contradict each other, then have Claude build it. Rerun the pilot-cohort brief with fresh data through it.
monday.who: Me first, then one person from my team of fourteen as a test pick-up.
monday.when: Monday morning for the first run, and send to the pricing working group by Wednesday.
monday.stop_condition: If the skeptic agent flags no contradiction I had not already seen after two rounds of pushback, I drop it.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context files, so everyone keeps their own copy.

misconception.why: The module says specifying well is the hard part and that the agent assembles the rest. The folder-count point also showed that the real constraint is uptake and shared context, and better prompts do not fix that. I still think prompt quality matters somewhat.

one_line: Good second half on citing sources and counting what people actually took up. The room exercise is long and the ending is a bit grand.
